title: Bhima keeps watch
hook: the city mourns the living, and in the forest Bhima holds his anger and keeps watch
carry: krodha, anger, is an enemy within
tomorrow: who rises out of a king's fire?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boat at the Ganga, carrying the family to the far bank. Your line: a tirtha is a crossing to the far shore.

In Hastinapura, the news arrives: the Pandavas are dead, burned at Varanavata with their mother. Dhritarashtra weeps, the text says, and orders the rites for the dead. Water is offered for them. The people mourn. Vidura grieves only a little, because he knows. Far away, the five brothers and their mother are alive, asleep on the ground. Two places, and two kinds of grief.

In the forest they've gone as far as they can. Kunti is exhausted and thirsty. Bhima goes for water, and by the time he's back they're all asleep on the bare ground under a tree. So Bhima sits up alone and looks at them. The text gives him a lament here. In paraphrase: what could hurt more than this, my brothers sleeping on the earth, my mother lying in the open. He thinks of Duryodhana, and his anger rises. He could go back and end it, he says. But Yudhishthira isn't angry, and Bhima won't move without him. So he stays, and keeps watch. Hinduism has a name for what Bhima is holding: krodha, anger. Many Hindu teachers count it among the six inner enemies, with desire, greed, delusion, pride and envy. And in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna traces how it ruins a person: from craving comes anger, from anger confusion, from confusion you forget what matters, and then your judgment goes, and you fall. Notice the teaching isn't that Bhima shouldn't feel it. His anger is about something real. The teaching is that it mustn't drive. The brother known for his strength doesn't crush his anger, and doesn't obey it. He sits with it, and turns its heat into keeping watch, so the others can rest. In the city, a king weeps for nephews his own son tried to kill. In the forest, the brother known for his temper spends it sitting still.
screen: `ASLEEP ON THE BARE GROUND.` · `BHIMA'S LAMENT, AND HIS ANGER.` · `KRODHA: AN INNER ENEMY.` · then, large: `ANGER FELT, NOT OBEYED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that makes you angry right now, something real. Notice where it sits: jaw, chest, hands. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Breathe out slowly. If you pray, say what many Hindus say at the end of a prayer: Om shanti, shanti, shanti, peace three times. If you don't, just breathe the heat down a little. Then picture someone asleep you'd watch over, and let that be where the strength goes.
Bhima, the brother known for strength and anger, who spends this night sitting still, keeping watch while his family sleeps.
Your line: krodha, anger, is an enemy within. Bhima felt it, and kept watch instead. Day seven hundred thirty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Offering water for the dead, called tarpana, is part of Hindu funeral and remembrance rites; in this story the offering is made for the Pandavas while they are still alive.

fork.setup: a friend asks: if Hindus call anger an enemy, was Bhima wrong to feel it? by the story, what fits?
options: no. feeling it is human; the teaching is not letting krodha drive, and he didn't.
yes. a good Hindu never feels anger at all.
no, and since he was in the right he should have gone back and fought.
fork.reveal: his lament and his anger are real in the text. he holds them, waits on Yudhishthira, and spends the night keeping watch.

original.note: Sanskrit krodha: anger, counted among the six inner enemies; what Bhima holds under the tree.

chat.says: the old landlord is keeping our WHOLE deposit 😡 i wanted to go yell at him. dad said 'krodha, beta' and made me sit down. ok but i'm RIGHT??
options: you can be right and still not let krodha drive. Bhima was furious and kept watch instead.
if you're right, anger is your dharma. go yell.
good Hindus never get angry, so just don't feel it.
chat.meaning: Bhima's anger at Duryodhana was real, but he held it and kept watch. Hindus count krodha among the inner enemies: feel it, don't let it drive.

tie.story: Bhima, furious at Duryodhana, sat up all night under a tree and kept watch over his sleeping family instead of going back.
tie.friend: Priya can be right about the deposit and still not let krodha drive: a calm letter to the landlord, not a shouting match.
tie.you: what anger are you carrying that could turn into watching over someone?

Hastinapura.meaning: the Kuru capital, where the court mourns the Pandavas

Dhritarashtra.meaning: the blind king, uncle of the Pandavas

Duryodhana.meaning: Dhritarashtra's eldest son, the Pandavas' rival cousin

Varanavata.meaning: the town where the house of lac burned

krodha.meaning: anger, one of the six inner enemies

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (the mourning at Hastinapura; Dhritarashtra's grief and the water rites; Vidura grieves little)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva, opening of Hidimba-vadha Parva (Bhima fetches water and keeps watch; his lament over his sleeping family)
Bhagavad Gita 2.62-63 (Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva): from dwelling on things comes attachment, then desire, then anger, then delusion, loss of memory and of judgment, and ruin
